newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour MPs set out positive case for EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour MPs set out positive case for EMU.

text.p: Joining a single currency would help any Labour government meet its social and economic goals by providing the stability needed to boost investment, growth and jobs, a group of 14 pro-European Labour MPs said on Thursday.
"It is very likely that the single currency will happen, and it is important that the positive case for British membership is more widely understood," member of parliament Giles Radice said.

At the launch of a pamphlet called "Jobs, Growth and Security," Radice said he was absolutely convinced that a majority of Labour MPs backed his group's view that joining a single currency would benefit Britain if the terms were right.

The pamphlet stopped short of explicitly calling for Britain to join a single currency, backing instead Labour leader Tony Blair's official line that the main opposition party should keep its options open. "To rule it out now would be a disaster for Britain, and indeed for our influence in Europe," Radice said.
The MPs made it clear that they would sign up for EMU as early as possible providing Britain met the Maastricht criteria and it was judged to be in the country's national interest.
"If the financial and economic criteria are right, political considerations around a single currency should not stand in the way of entry at the earliest opportunity," MP Keith Hill said.

The pamphlet opens by recalling that because of its late entry into the then Common Market, Britain was still paying the price for not having been able to influence negotiations for the Common Agricultural Policy. "We must not miss the boat again on the single currency," it says.

MP Mike Gapes said that Britain would pay a heavy price for not joining a single currency because investors, fearing devaluation, would demand a big interest rate premium to hold sterling. That could mean, paradoxically, the government following deflationary policies for the privilege of staying outside a zone of lower interest rates and currency stability.
"We could be sleep-walking into disaster if we don't seriously take into account the implications of a single currency," Gapes said. "We cannot behave as if it's not going to happen."
Radice played down the fact that only 14 Labour MPs had backed the pamphlet, whereas 50 had signed up to a campaign opposing membership of the single currency.
"We're not in the numbers game," he said, adding that he did not expect Labour to adopt a more Euro-sceptical line in the run-up to the general election, due by next May.
